summary: Christmas Day. The chronology records nothing else for Roosevelt.

headline: Alice stays in the city for the session
summary: Alice is urged to remain in New York City during the coming legislative term, while Roosevelt keeps company with his Assembly allies Isaac Hunt and William O'Neil. He has also shaved off his sideburns.

events.detail: Alice is urged to remain in New York City while the Assembly sits
Spends his time among his Assembly companions
Shaves off his sideburns

uncertain: Part of the record for this date is hard to read, including a cut-off line about economic and working conditions. Hunt's and O'Neil's first names come from context.

headline: Republicans name him for Speaker
summary: In Albany, Roosevelt wins the Republican caucus nomination for Speaker of the Assembly, put forward by Isaac Hunt. The Stalwart faction fought him hard, but the Independents held and he carried the vote two to one.

events.detail: Wins the Republican caucus nomination for Assembly Speaker over Stalwart opposition
Records in his diary his impressions of his rural Republican backers and colleagues

tr_quotes.text: I received the complimentary Republican nomination [made by Issac Hunt] for Speaker of the Assembly. The Stalwarts made a strong fight against me; but the Independents stood firm, and we beat them two to one.
Hunt, a lean, meloncholy, humorous yankee, and O'Neil, a bright, straight forward backwoodsman, were my two main backers.
Howe, my colleague from New York is a very good man; a gentleman of broad culture.

uncertain: Howe's first name (Walter) and O'Neil's (William) come from context; the bracketed name in the quote was added by the record's compiler.

headline: Chapin elected Speaker; Roosevelt leads the minority
summary: The Democratic majority makes Alfred C. Chapin of Brooklyn Speaker, 84 votes to Roosevelt's 44, leaving Roosevelt as Republican minority leader. He is named to the Cities, Militia, Rules, and Privileges and Elections committees, and the last group heads to New York to hear disputed seats.

events.detail: Loses the Speakership vote to Chapin, 84 to 44, and becomes minority leader
Named to committees on Cities, Militia, Rules, and Privileges and Elections
Privileges and Elections committee goes to New York City to take up contested seats

tr_quotes.text: The Legislature organized, and the Democratic majority elected as speaker Chapin of Brooklyn, by all odds the ablest man on either side of the House
Chapin appointed a committee on priviledges and elections, of which I am one, to hear the cases of the contestants for seats. The committee went down to New York.

uncertain: Chapin's full name supplied from context.

headline: Home by the fire with Alice
summary: Back in New York, Roosevelt delights in an evening at home with Alice: a coal fire, his books around him, and a game of backgammon in their small sitting room.

events.detail: Spends the evening at home with his wife Alice playing backgammon

tr_quotes.text: Back again in my own lovely little home, with the sweetest and prettiest of all little wives - my own sunny darling. I can imagine nothing more happy in life than an evening spent in my cosy little sitting room, before a bright fire of soft coal, my books all around me, and playing backgammon with my own dainty mistress.

headline: Hearing the Sprague–Bliss election contest
summary: Roosevelt's committee takes testimony in New York City on the disputed election between Henry Sprague and his opponent Bliss. Roosevelt is convinced Sprague was cheated out of the count.

events.detail: Committee hears evidence in the Sprague–Bliss contested seat

tr_quotes.text: Today we heard the evidence in the case of the contested election between Sprague and Bliss. The former was counted out beyond a shadow of doubt.

headline: Militia drill and Aunt Annie's theatricals

events.detail: Drills Company B of the 8th Regiment

tr_quotes.text: Went to drill my company (B. of the 8th Regiment) as usual.

headline: Sifting the Brooklyn election testimony
summary: For a second straight day, Roosevelt's committee works through testimony in the Brooklyn contested-seat cases, which he finds riddled with perjury.

events.detail: Committee continues hearing the Brooklyn contested-election cases

tr_quotes.text: All through to day, as also yesterday, the committee has been wading through the mass of perjury involved in the Brooklyn contested election cases.

headline: Church, family dinner, tea with Mittie

events.detail: Attends morning service at Dr. Hall's church

tr_quotes.text: Church in the morning at Dr. Halls. The family dinner was at our house: in the evening we took tea with motherling.

headline: Passes his exam for captain

events.detail: Committee sits through the day

tr_quotes.text: Committee sat all day. In evening passed my examination for Captain in the 8th.

headline: Back to Albany; sizing up colleagues
summary: Roosevelt returns to Albany as Speaker Chapin names his committees. In his diary he sketches his fellow members, from the conceited Assemblyman House to white-bearded old Cleavland, and notes that he, Hunt, O'Neil and Howe share neighboring seats.

events.detail: Returns from New York City to Albany
Speaker Chapin announces committee assignments
Diary portraits of Assembly colleagues

tr_quotes.text: Crane, of my New York colleagues, is honest but light weight; House is marvellously conceited and noisy. I think he will prove a nuisnance [sic].
Old Cleavland is a very fine fellow, with a grand head, his hair and beard both snow white.
Hunt, O Neil, Howe and myself sit together a pleasant quartette.

headline: Beats the Stalwarts again
summary: Roosevelt defeats the Stalwarts a second time in caucus, securing the regent nomination for his candidate Matthew Hale. On the Assembly floor he trades blows with Murphy and Tim Campbell and comes out ahead.

events.detail: Wins caucus fight to nominate Matthew Hale as regent

tr_quotes.text: Had another fight with the stalwarts in the caucus to nominate a regent, and beat them again, my nominee, Matthew Hale receiving the somewhat empty honor.
On the floor of the house I openned [sic] the session by a brush with Murphy + 'Tim' Campbell, and got the better of those 'renowned leaders'.

headline: Warns of public anger at great corporations

tr_quotes.text: There is a strong and growing feeling of indignation among the people at the actions of these great corporations . . . it is incumbent upon us to see that this feeling takes a lawful shade.
If it becomes evident that these great public robbers cannot be reached by law, then among the people at large the temptation to take action that is outside the law becomes very strong.

For the sake of protecting honest capital, we ought to punish, if we legally can, the deeds of the dishonest wealthy for fear that someday an uprising might come that will overwhelm innocent and guilty alike.
